script.title: Why the Royal Navy Plated Ships with Copper

lines: Charles Middleton carried a model warship with a copper bottom to the King.
Wooden hulls were under continuous attack.
Shipworm attacked their timber. Weed grew rapidly and slowed ships.
In 1761, the Navy coppered the entire bottom of HMS Alarm.
In the West Indies, worms had eaten into her wooden hull.
The copper performed very well.
But the copper reacted with the iron bolts holding the ship together.
Many bolts became nearly useless.
In 1766, the Navy removed Alarm's copper.
Then in 1778, France declared war on Britain.
Middleton had to supply over 100 ships.
Building one warship could take five years and 2000 trees.
You see, it's like soap in the shower. Its surface keeps washing away, so nothing sticks.
In seawater, copper makes a thin poisonous film.
The film slowly washes away, so worms and weed cannot attach.
A coppered ship could stay at sea much longer without cleaning or repairs.
Coppering one big warship cost £1,500, compared to £262 for wood.
The King backed Middleton anyway.
By 1781, 82 ships of the line had been coppered.
Merchants copied it, and Lloyd's of London charged coppered ships lower insurance.
That is where the phrase copper-bottomed comes from.

claims.claim: Middleton petitioned King George III directly and took with him a model of HMS Bellona showing a coppered bottom; the King backed him for an expensive process for an untested technology.
Ships' hulls were under continuous attack by shipworm, barnacles and other marine growth; weed grew rapidly and slowed ships.
In 1761 the 32-gun frigate HMS Alarm was ordered to have her entire bottom coppered after the worms had taken a significant toll on her wooden hull in the West Indies; the copper performed very well.
The copper bolts reacted with the iron bolts, rendering many bolts nearly useless; in 1766 Alarm's copper was removed.
In 1778 France declared war on Britain to support the American rebels; Middleton had to supply over 100 ships; it could take five years and 2000 trees to build a warship.

In contact with water the copper produced a poisonous film that was slightly soluble and gradually washed away, leaving no way for marine life to attach; coppering let the navy stay at sea much longer without cleaning and repairs.
The metal to copper a 74-gun ship cost £1,500, compared to £262 for wood; by 1781, 82 ships of the line had been coppered.
Lloyd's of London charged lower insurance premiums for coppered vessels; from this stems the phrase copper-bottomed.

cast.middleton: a 52 year old English naval administrator, tall and gaunt, a long pale face with a hooked nose, grey powdered hair tied back with a black ribbon, wearing a plain chocolate brown frock coat, a buff waistcoat and a white neckcloth, 1770s
cast.king: a 40 year old English king, plump, a round fleshy pink face, pale blue eyes, a white powdered wig with side curls, wearing a scarlet velvet coat embroidered with gold, a pale blue sash and a white lace cravat, 1770s
cast.carpenter: a 30 year old English ship carpenter, wiry, a sunburned face with a crooked nose, short black curly hair, a short black beard, wearing a rust orange wool shirt with rolled sleeves and a leather apron, 1760s
cast.captain: a 45 year old Royal Navy captain, stocky, a weathered ruddy face with heavy grey eyebrows, a white tied-back wig, wearing a dark navy coat with white lapels, gold buttons and a black tricorn hat, 1760s
